sun and moon work against each other, leading to neap tides with smaller differences between high and low water. Local geography significantly
shapes tidal patterns, where bays and shelves can amplify fluctuations while open oceans see less variation. Beyond moving water, tides

shape coastlines, influence marine life, and have historically been harnessed for fishing and energy generation.

gravitational pull of the moon and the sun on Earth's waters. As the moon orbits our planet, its
gravity draws the ocean toward it, creating a bulge of water on the side facing the
moon. Simultaneously, inertia creates a second bulge on the opposite side of the Earth, resulting in
two high tides each day. The sun also exerts a gravitational force, though its greater distance makes its effect
roughly half that of the moon's. When the sun, moon, and Earth align
during full and new moons, their combined gravitational forces produce spring tides,
characterized by higher high tides and lower low tides. Conversely, during the first and
third quarters of the moon, the sun and moon work against each other,
leading to neap tides with smaller differences between high and low water. Local geography significantly shapes
tidal patterns, where bays and shelves can amplify fluctuations while open oceans see less variation.
Beyond moving water, tides shape coastlines, influence marine life, and have historically

been harnessed for fishing and energy generation.
